lessonRef.subject: financial-literacy
lessonRef.title: Launch and diagnostic: risk return liquidity and time horizon
lessonRef.focus: risk return liquidity and time horizon

objective: Learners compare invented returns on saving and investing and weigh them against the liquidity a near-term need requires.
scenario: Perrine is a made-up eighth grader comparing two pretend homes for $10,000.00: an invented savings account paying 1% a year and an invented investment averaging 7% a year but able to fall. She may need the money in six months.
safetyNotes: Every amount, person, business, and account in this task is invented for practice. Nothing here refers to a real household.
Never write a real bank account, card, PIN, password, Social Security, or tax number on this sheet; the task never asks for one.
This is education, not individualized financial advice. Real money decisions belong to a trusted adult.
These rates are invented for the exercise and are not a recommendation about any real product.

tasks.directions: Compute one simulated year on Perrine's invented savings account at 1%.

prompts.text: What does the savings account pay in a year?

tasks.directions: Compute a year at the invented 7% average and find the difference for Perrine.

prompts.text: What would a year at 7% produce?
How much larger is the invested return in a year?

tasks.directions: Model the case where Perrine must withdraw after a year in which the investment falls 12%.

prompts.text: What would the $10,000.00 be worth after a 12% fall?
How much worse off is that than the savings account after a year?

tasks.directions: The money may be needed in six months.

prompts.text: Using Perrine's figures, explain why a near-term need changes the answer even though the investment has the higher average return.

remediation: If a learner treats the average return as guaranteed, require the fall scenario to be computed in full for Perrine, written beside the average-return figure, before any recommendation is stated, so the range of outcomes is visible rather than a single expected number.
extension: Ask the learner what horizon would change the recommendation for Perrine, and to justify it.
